claims.claim: In the HIP ATTACK trial (2970 people with hip fracture, 69 hospitals, 17 countries), surgery at a median of 6 hours after diagnosis did not reduce deaths or major complications at 90 days compared with standard care at a median of 24 hours.
claims.supporting_passage: "HIP ATTACK was an international, randomised, controlled trial done at 69 hospitals in 17 countries. Patients with a hip fracture that required surgery and were aged 45 years or older were eligible." ... "2970 of these were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive accelerated surgery (n=1487) or standard care (n=1483). The median time from hip fracture diagnosis to surgery was 6 h (IQR 4-9) in the accelerated-surgery group and 24 h (10-42) in the standard-care group (p<0·0001). 140 (9%) patients assigned to accelerated surgery and 154 (10%) assigned to standard care died, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0·91 (95% CI 0·72 to 1·14) and absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 1% (-1 to 3; p=0·40). Major complications occurred in 321 (22%) patients assigned to accelerated surgery and 331 (22%) assigned to standard care, with an HR of 0·97 (0·83 to 1·13) and an ARR of 1% (-2 to 4; p=0·71)." Interpretation: "Among patients with a hip fracture, accelerated surgery did not significantly lower the risk of mortality or a composite of major complications compared with standard care."
claims.location: Abstract (Methods, Findings, Interpretation)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 45+ with hip fracture needing surgery (69 hospitals, 17 countries) / accelerated surgery, goal within 6 h of diagnosis / standard care / co-primary: death; composite of death, MI, stroke, VTE, sepsis, pneumonia, life-threatening or major bleeding / 90 days after randomisation
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of about 3,000 people with a broken hip in 17 countries, operating within about 6 hours of diagnosis did not clearly reduce deaths or serious complications compared with usual care, where half had surgery within about 24 hours. At 90 days, about 9 in 100 had died in the fast group and 10 in 100 in the usual-care group; serious complications affected about 22 in 100 in both.
claims.qualifications: Did not show a clear difference; the uncertainty range runs from about 1 fewer to 3 more deaths per 100 prevented, so a small benefit or none is possible. Times are from diagnosis, not from admission. Say 'did not clearly reduce', not 'no benefit'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Secondary outcomes favoured accelerated surgery (see C03-17-b). Observational data link longer waits with more deaths (C03-17-c). Trial participants were those eligible and consenting (7780 eligible of 27,701 screened; 2970 enrolled).

trial setting

claims.claim: In HIP ATTACK, accelerated surgery did not harm patients, and it was linked with faster mobilisation after surgery, a shorter hospital stay and less postoperative confusion (secondary outcomes).
claims.supporting_passage: "This study found that accelerated surgery (within a goal of 6 h after diagnosis) did not improve either mortality or non-fatal major complications (myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism, sepsis, pneumonia, life-threatening bleeding and major bleeding) 90 days later among 1487 people with hip fracture, compared with a similar number (n = 1483) who received standard care (median time from diagnosis to surgery of 24 h (IQR 10–42). Accelerated surgery did not harm patients, even for those with acute medical conditions. Interestingly, accelerated surgery significantly reduced both the prevalence of postoperative delirium (9% vs. 12%, HR 0.72 (95%CI 0.58–0.92), p = 0.0089) and length of inpatient stay, and improved the speed of postoperative mobilisation. The Working Party considers these data re-assuring and clinically important for patients but acknowledge that the resource implications of accelerated surgery need to be calculated before recommending its adoption into current UK practice."
claims.location: Griffiths 2021 guideline, full text, Controversies section (surgical delay); passage spanned two retrieved text chunks at '0.58–0' / '.92'
claims.pico_timeframe: As HIP ATTACK; secondary outcomes as summarised by the Association of Anaesthetists working party
claims.safe_wording: The fast-surgery group did get up and about sooner after the operation and left hospital sooner, and the trial found no sign that operating that fast caused harm.
claims.qualifications: Verified through the Association of Anaesthetists guideline's summary, not the trial paper itself (Lancet full text not accessible). Secondary outcomes, so treat as supportive rather than definitive. Less pain was claimed by the judge but was NOT verified; do not state it. Delirium is excluded as a topic: the post can say 'less confusion after surgery' at most, and need not mention it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The guideline says the resource implications of accelerated surgery need to be calculated before recommending it for UK practice, and continues to recommend a 36-hour limit.

numbers.meaning: postoperative delirium, accelerated vs standard (secondary outcome; HR 0.72); optional, topic excluded

claims.claim: In a large Ontario cohort, waiting more than 24 hours for hip fracture surgery was linked with a small increase in 30-day deaths (association, not proof of cause).
claims.supporting_passage: "Among 42 230 patients with hip fracture (mean [SD] age, 80.1 years [10.7], 70.5% women) who met study entry criteria, overall mortality at 30 days was 7.0%. The risk of complications increased when wait times were greater than 24 hours, irrespective of the complication considered. Compared with 13 731 propensity-score matched patients who received surgery earlier, 13 731 patients who received surgery after 24 hours had a significantly higher risk of 30-day mortality (898 [6.5%] vs 790 [5.8%]; % absolute RD, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.23-1.35) and the composite outcome (1680 [12.2%]) vs 1383 [10.1%]; % absolute RD, 2.16; 95% CI, 1.43-2.89)." Conclusion: "Among adults undergoing hip fracture surgery, increased wait time was associated with a greater risk of 30-day mortality and other complications. A wait time of 24 hours may represent a threshold defining higher risk."
claims.location: Abstract (Results, Conclusions)
claims.pico_timeframe: 42,230 adults having hip fracture surgery, 72 Ontario hospitals, 2009 to 2014 / surgery more than 24 h after hospital arrival / surgery within 24 h (propensity matched) / 30-day mortality; composite of death, MI, DVT, PE, pneumonia / 30 days
claims.safe_wording: In a study of over 40,000 people in Ontario, those who waited more than 24 hours for surgery were slightly more likely to die within 30 days: about 6.5 in 100 compared with 5.8 in 100 among similar people operated on sooner. This is a link, and it does not prove that the wait caused the deaths.
claims.qualifications: Observational; adjusted and propensity matched but residual confounding possible (people who wait may be sicker). Absolute difference under 1 percentage point. Timing from hospital arrival (HIP ATTACK timed from diagnosis). Use 'linked with', not 'causes' or 'leads to'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: HIP ATTACK found no clear mortality benefit from going much faster than about 24 h; the two findings answer different questions (avoidable delay beyond a day vs racing within hours).

wait time above which complication risk rose (spline inflection point)

claims.claim: The Association of Anaesthetists does not recommend delaying hip fracture surgery to wait for an echocardiogram.
claims.supporting_passage: "Valvular heart disease occurs in approximately 10% hip fracture patients in the UK [19]. However, delay to hip fracture surgery for diagnostic echocardiography also increases postoperative mortality." ... "However, the treatment of any valvular disease is very unlikely to precede surgery in the surgical population with hip fracture, and it remains unlikely that the results of echocardiography will inform a change in the anaesthetic management of patients with suspected valvular heart disease. The Working Party does not recommend delaying surgery pending echocardiography. Instead, management should continue to involve carefully administered, (invasively) monitored general or spinal anaesthesia, which aims to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion pressures, with possible short-term admission to a higher-level care unit postoperatively."
claims.location: Griffiths 2021, full text, Controversies (echocardiography)
claims.pico_timeframe: People with hip fracture and suspected valvular heart disease, UK
claims.safe_wording: UK anaesthetic guidance says not to delay surgery while waiting for a heart scan (echocardiogram); the result rarely changes how the anaesthetic is given, and the heart valve problem is very unlikely to be treated before the hip.
claims.qualifications: The guideline acknowledges echocardiography can quantify disease, and notes conflicting studies and a possible future RCT. The guidance still expects careful, monitored anaesthesia and possible higher-level care after surgery.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Studies since 2011 gave conflicting results on pre-operative focused echocardiography (guideline refs 54 to 58).

"The 2011 guidance advised that surgery should not be delayed in patients taking aspirin, clopidogrel or warfarin, provided vitamin K-assisted reversal of the latter reduced the international normalised ratio below 2 for surgery and 1.5 for spinal anaesthesia." ... "Data suggest that the use of anticoagulants/antiplatelet therapies is associated with a slightly increased risk of peri-operative transfusion in hip fracture patients but no increase in mortality [60–62]." ... "Abrupt cessation of such medication and failure to restart it postoperatively can expose the person to increased risks of cardiac ischaemia and stent occlusion, cerebrovascular accident [65] and limb ischaemia." Doleman 2015 abstract: "For patients taking clopidogrel undergoing early surgery, there was no associated increase in overall mortality (OR 0.89; 95% CI: 0.58-1.38) or 30-day mortality (OR 1.10 95% CI: 0.48-2.54). However, there was an associated increase in blood transfusion (OR 1.41 95% CI: 1.00-1.99)." ... "Early surgery appears safe for patients with hip fracture though there may be a small increase in the rate of blood transfusion. However, larger prospective trials are required to confirm these findings."
claims.location: Griffiths 2021 full text, Controversies (anticoagulant and antiplatelet management); Doleman 2015 abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Hip fracture patients taking aspirin or clopidogrel / early surgery / patients not on antiplatelets or delayed surgery / transfusion, mortality / peri-operative
claims.safe_wording: Association of Anaesthetists guidance has advised since 2011 that surgery should not be delayed because someone takes aspirin or clopidogrel. Studies of people on clopidogrel who had early surgery found slightly more blood transfusions but no rise in deaths.
claims.qualifications: The 2020 guideline's main text restates the 2011 advice and moves detailed antiplatelet/anticoagulant recommendations to Appendix S1, which was not opened; attribute to 'Association of Anaesthetists guidance (2011, restated in the 2020 update)'. Meta-analysis evidence is observational. Stopping antiplatelets abruptly carries its own risks (stents, stroke). Warfarin is an anticoagulant and needs reversal; do not group it with antiplatelets. Spinal anaesthesia decisions in people on antiplatelets are the anaesthetist's call.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Doleman found a borderline increase in transfusion (OR 1.41, CI 1.00 to 1.99); other meta-analyses (Yang 2020, Soo 2016; abstracts seen) reach the same overall conclusion.

numbers.meaning: UK hip fracture patients taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs before surgery (per guideline)
overall mortality, clopidogrel users with early surgery vs non-users (observational; not significant); do not convert to 'times more likely'

claims.claim: People on direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are a separate case with specific guidance; in England and Wales in 2018 about 3% of hip fracture patients were delayed more than 36 hours by DOAC therapy or warfarin reversal, and almost all DOAC users were delayed beyond 36 hours.
claims.supporting_passage: "Direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC), such as rivaroxaban, apixaban and dabigatran, were introduced into the UK in 2008, but their prescription increased more markedly after 2012 and so were not considered in the 2011 guidance. Approximately 2% of UK hip fracture patients currently take DOACs." ... "There are significant and progressive mortality and morbidity risks associated with delay to surgery beyond 24(–48) h in hip fracture patients [68, 69]. In 2018, approximately 3% of hip fracture patients in England and Wales were delayed > 36 h before surgery as a result of their DOAC therapy or for warfarin reversal; virtually all patients taking DOACs were delayed > 36 h before surgery [6]. Mindful of these risks and in recognition of other Association of Anaesthetists' guidance, the Working Party has developed comprehensive recommendations for the management of patients with hip fracture who are taking antiplatelet/anticoagulant medication pre-operatively. These can be found in online Supporting Information, Appendix S1, together with a one-page summary..."
claims.location: Griffiths 2021 full text, Controversies (anticoagulant and antiplatelet management)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK hip fracture patients on DOACs or warfarin; national data for 2018 (England and Wales) as cited by the guideline
claims.safe_wording: Blood thinners of the DOAC type (such as apixaban or rivaroxaban) are handled differently: the Association of Anaesthetists publishes specific advice on timing. In 2018, almost everyone in England and Wales taking a DOAC waited more than 36 hours for hip fracture surgery. Ask the anaesthetist or orthogeriatrician what the plan is and when surgery can go ahead.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's claim that DOAC timing 'depends on the drug, dose and kidney function' was NOT verified (Appendix S1 not opened); do not state it. The 3% figure is a national figure cited by the guideline (ref 6), not a trial result; it is 2018 data. The 2020 text says DOAC users were about 2% of UK hip fracture patients.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Practice may have changed since 2018; no newer figure was checked.

numbers.meaning: UK hip fracture patients taking DOACs (per 2020 guideline)
hip fracture patients in England and Wales delayed >36 h by DOAC therapy or warfarin reversal, 2018

claims.claim: Guidance expects medical problems to be corrected proactively within the 36-hour window, with the team told what needs to happen and decisions documented, rather than surgery cancelled on the day for a single abnormal value.
claims.supporting_passage: Griffiths 2021: "In many cases, the risks of delay associated with pain and immobility contribute to poor outcomes to a far greater extent than correction of an abnormality to a particular numerical value. Rather than cancelling surgery on the day of operation in reaction to one of the seven abnormalities listed, the Working Party considers that 36 h (or less) provides sufficient time for the proactive involvement of anaesthetists in correcting medical obstacles to surgery. In the (rare) event of cancellation for medical reasons, patients should be kept under 12-hourly assessment by anaesthetic teams. Anaesthetists should work with orthogeriatricians to optimise the person for surgery as soon as possible, communicate with the hip fracture care team what needs to happen to avoid repeated cancellation and delay, and document any decisions clearly in the person's medical notes." Scottish standards, Standard 6: "Hip fracture patients are likely to have multiple co-morbidities, however in general surgery should not be delayed unless 'the benefits of additional medical treatment outweigh the risks of delaying surgery'. [23] Thirty-six hours (or less) is a sufficient period to allow for correction or reduction of medical obstacles to surgery, provided this is instigated immediately at presentation. [24]"
claims.location: Griffiths 2021 Controversies (surgical delay); Scottish standards Standard 6 rationale
claims.pico_timeframe: UK hip fracture pathway, pre-operative period
claims.safe_wording: UK guidance says surgery should be delayed only if the benefit of more medical treatment outweighs the risk of waiting, that 36 hours is enough time to correct most problems if work starts at once, and that the team should say what needs to happen and write the decision down.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's position that 'any delay should name the specific correctable problem and when it will be corrected' is a reasonable reading of this guidance ('communicate ... what needs to happen', 'document any decisions') but the time-by-when element is an editorial judgement; mark it as 'we should' rather than as a guideline quotation. The angle's claim that delays 'often turn out' to be waits for tests or drugs to wear off is NOT supported by any opened source; drop it or replace with the DOAC figure (C03-21-e).

numbers.meaning: window guidance considers sufficient to correct medical obstacles
anaesthetic reassessment if surgery is cancelled for medical reasons

claims.claim: The Association of Anaesthetists' 2011 guidance listed seven 'acceptable' reasons for delaying surgery, each with a threshold (for example haemoglobin below 80 g/L, heart rate above 120 with a correctable arrhythmia).
claims.supporting_passage: "The 2011 guidelines list seven 'acceptable' reasons for delaying surgery: 1Haemoglobin < 80 g.l−1 2Plasma sodium concentration < 120 or > 150 mmol.l−1 and potassium concentration < 2.8 or > 6.0 mmol−1 3Uncontrolled diabetes 4Uncontrolled or acute onset left ventricular failure. 5Correctable cardiac arrhythmia with a ventricular rate > 120.min−1 6Chest infection with sepsis 7Reversible coagulopathy The Fragility Fracture Network guidance states “surgery should be delayed only if the benefits of additional medical treatment outweigh the risks of delaying surgery”."
claims.location: Griffiths 2021 full text, Controversies (surgical delay)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK anaesthetic guidance 2011 as restated in 2020
claims.safe_wording: The 2011 anaesthetic guidance gave seven reasons that could justify a delay, each with a cut-off, such as haemoglobin below 80 g/L or a correctable fast heart rhythm above 120 beats a minute. The 2020 update says these should be corrected within the 36 hours rather than used to cancel on the day.
claims.qualifications: Optional detail for a practitioner post; if used, pair it with the 2020 update's reframing (C03-21-f).

numbers.meaning: 'acceptable' reasons for delay in 2011 guidance

numbers.value: Hb < 80 g/L; Na < 120 or > 150 mmol/L; K < 2.8 or > 6.0 mmol/L; ventricular rate > 120/min
numbers.meaning: 2011 thresholds

claims.claim: In England and Wales, being next of kin does not by itself give legal power to consent to an operation for an adult who lacks capacity: the decision-maker is someone the person appointed through a lasting power of attorney (health and welfare), or a court-appointed deputy; otherwise it is usually the responsible clinician, who decides in the person's best interests.
claims.supporting_passage: Wade and Kitzinger 2019 abstract: "Context: The legal framework is the Mental Capacity Act (MCA) 2005, which applies to England and Wales. Theory: Unless there is a valid and applicable Advance Decision, an appointed decision-maker needs to decide for those without capacity. This may be someone appointed by the patient through a Lasting Power of Attorney, or a Deputy appointed by the court. Otherwise the decision-maker is usually the responsible clinician." Orr and Baruah 2018: "If a patient is unable to consent, treatment is carried out in their best interests." ... "A patient may have an advanced decision, lasting power of attorney for health and welfare (LPA) or a court-appointed deputy." Zalmay 2021: "The Consent Form Four (CF) is filled out when treatment is offered to a patient who is deemed to lack the capacity to be involved in this decision-making. Within it, a section entitled 'Involvement of those close to the patient' outlines that the clinician taking consent should seek the views of those close to the patient, and requires them to document this discussion (Appendix 1]. This is part of the best-interests decision-making process as outlined by the Mental Capacity Act 2005 []."
claims.location: Wade 2019 abstract (Context, Theory); Orr 2018 full text, 'The Mental Capacity Act 2005'; Zalmay 2021 full text, Introduction
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults (16+) lacking capacity for a treatment decision, England and Wales, MCA 2005
claims.safe_wording: In England and Wales, being next of kin does not give you the legal right to consent to an operation for your mother. If she can't decide for herself, the decision is made by someone she appointed under a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare, or a court-appointed deputy. If there is no one like that, the doctor responsible makes the decision in her best interests.
claims.qualifications: Say 'usually the responsible clinician' or 'the doctor responsible'. An LPA must be registered to be used (Orr 2018). None of these can compel treatment that is not in the person's best interests. Do not describe the Northern Ireland process (editor's instruction). Do not claim how often relatives are wrongly asked to sign: no opened source measures it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Wade and Kitzinger note that 'The MCA is often not followed in healthcare settings, despite widespread mandatory training' and that there is often 'lack of clarity about who is the responsible decision-maker'.

claims.claim: Under the Mental Capacity Act, family and close friends must be consulted (if time permits) and the person's own wishes and values inform the best-interests decision.
claims.supporting_passage: Orr and Baruah 2018: "If a patient is unable to consent, treatment is carried out in their best interests. Assessment of best interests must include social, psychological, and medical factors and should be informed by the patient's attitudes and opinions. If time permits, family or close friends must be consulted. If this is not possible, and the course of action proposed may have serious consequences or the risks and benefits are finely balanced, an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate should be consulted." Wade and Kitzinger 2019: "Once persistent lack of capacity is confirmed, an early meeting should be arranged with family and friends, to start a process of sharing information about the patient's medical condition and their values, wishes, feelings and beliefs with a view to making timely treatment decisions in the patient's best interests." Zalmay 2021: "When a patient is judged to lack the capacity to consent to a procedure, the Mental Capacity Act outlines that where appropriate, the clinician should seek the views of those interested in their welfare, usually referring to their NoK or lasting power of attorney []."
claims.location: Orr 2018 full text ('The Mental Capacity Act 2005'); Wade 2019 abstract (Solution); Zalmay 2021 full text (Intervention design)
claims.pico_timeframe: As above
claims.safe_wording: The team must still ask you about her. The law expects the decision to take account of what she would want, her values and her beliefs, and family or close friends should be consulted if there is time.
claims.qualifications: 'If time permits': in an emergency the consultation may be brief or not possible. The Wade 2019 'early meeting' is a recommendation from that review, not a legal requirement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Zalmay 2021 found gaps in practice at one hospital (C03-09-e).

claims.claim: In Scotland, the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 gives doctors general authority to treat an adult who can't consent once a certificate of incapacity is completed; but if the person has a welfare attorney with power over medical decisions, the doctor must seek that attorney's consent where reasonable and practicable.
claims.supporting_passage: "The Act gives a 'general authority' to healthcare practitioners to treat a patient who is incapable of consenting to treatment provided that a certificate of incapacity has been completed (Fig. 1), and provided that the treatment falls within the general principles of the Act. Medical treatment is defined as 'any procedure or treatment designed to safeguard or promote physical or mental health'. If the patient is known to have appointed a proxy decision maker who has been granted power of attorney to make decisions regarding welfare, this general authority does not apply and the practitioner issuing the certificate must seek the consent of the welfare power of attorney before commencing treatment, where it is reasonable and practicable to do so. In an emergency, common law authority to provide treatment for the emergency preservation of life remains in place and completion of a certificate is not required to render this emergency treatment lawful."
claims.location: Edwardson and Baruah 2018, full text, 'Mental capacity in Scots law'
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults (16+) lacking capacity, Scotland, AWI (Scotland) Act 2000 Part 5
claims.safe_wording: In Scotland the law is different. If she can't decide, a doctor completes a certificate of incapacity, which allows treatment. But if she has appointed a welfare attorney with power over medical decisions, the doctor must ask for that attorney's consent where it is reasonable and practicable.
claims.qualifications: Welfare attorney consent is verified. The editor's wording that a court-appointed guardian with medical treatment powers can also consent was NOT verified in an opened source (the opened text lists guardians only among people to be consulted); either omit guardians or phrase as 'a welfare attorney (or a guardian with powers over medical treatment)' only after the editor accepts that it rests on the statute, which was not opened. Emergency life-saving treatment does not need a certificate. Do not describe Northern Ireland.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The AWI Act and its Part 5 code of practice were not opened; wording relies on a peer-reviewed BJA Education summary.

claims.claim: In Scotland, any treatment under the Act must take account of the person's past and present wishes and feelings, and involve consultation with specified people, including any guardian or welfare attorney; there is a presumption of capacity.
claims.supporting_passage: "In Scots law, there is a presumption that adults are legally capable of making decisions for themselves [presumption of capacity also applies to the Mental Capacity Act (2005) in England and Wales]." ... "The general principles of the Act are laid out in Section 1. This states that an intervention carried out under the Act: (i) should achieve a benefit not otherwise achievable; (ii) is the least restrictive option (i.e. the action made or decision taken should be the minimum necessary to achieve the intended purpose); (iii) account is taken of past and present expressed wishes and feelings as far as this is practicable; (iv) there is consultation with another specified person as far as is reasonable and practicable. Specified persons include a guardian or welfare attorney."
claims.location: Edwardson and Baruah 2018, full text, 'Mental capacity in Scots law'
claims.pico_timeframe: As above
claims.safe_wording: In Scotland too, the law says her past and present wishes and feelings must be taken into account, and certain people must be consulted.
claims.qualifications: The opened text says specified persons 'include' a guardian or welfare attorney; it does not list the nearest relative or carer explicitly, so the post should not say the law names relatives in Scotland.

claims.claim: Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate; a person who can communicate with help is not incapable for that reason alone, so it is fair to ask whether she could decide with help and time.
claims.supporting_passage: Orr and Baruah 2018: "A patient may lack capacity to make decisions about some aspects of their care but retain the capacity to make decisions about more straightforward aspects." ... "This decision confirms that capacity is time-and decision-specific and can fluctuate." Edwardson and Baruah 2018: "If this inability to communicate can be overcome with human or mechanical aids, it does not constitute incapacity for the purposes of the Act."
claims.location: Orr 2018 full text ('Consent: ethical principles'; 'Capacity: evolution of case law'); Edwardson 2018 full text
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults, UK law
claims.safe_wording: Capacity is about one decision at one time. A person may be able to make some decisions but not others, and it can change from hour to hour. You can ask whether she could decide for herself with help, or later in the day.
claims.qualifications: Hip fracture surgery is time-critical; waiting for capacity to return has to be weighed against the harm of delay. Do not imply surgery should wait indefinitely.

claims.claim: At one English hospital, before a feedback intervention, only 80% of people with hip fracture who lacked capacity had a documented attempt to contact their next of kin before surgery, and the next-of-kin section of Consent Form Four was completed in 30%.
claims.supporting_passage: "Pre-intervention, 80% (24/30) were noted to have had documented attempts at contacting their NoK prior to surgery. The section of Consent Form Four regarding the NoK discussion was completed in 30% (10/30). Following the intervention, all 28 patients had documented attempts at contacting their NoK prior to going for hip surgery, a significant improvement (p <0.05). The Consent Form Four NoK section was appropriately completed in 64.3% (18/28) (p <0.05)." Limitations: "A major limitation of this project was that we measured the documentation of attempts to contact next of kin; the actual rates of clinicians contacting next of kin may have been higher."
claims.location: Zalmay 2021, full text, Results and Limitations
claims.pico_timeframe: Hip fracture patients with AMTS < 8 lacking capacity, one 520-bed district general hospital in England; June to October 2019 (n=30) vs May to September 2020 (n=28)
claims.safe_wording: At one English hospital, notes showed an attempt to contact the family before surgery for 24 of 30 people who couldn't consent, and the family section of the consent form was filled in for 10 of 30. After the team was given feedback, contact attempts were recorded for all 28 people in the next group.
claims.qualifications: One hospital, small numbers, documentation rather than actual conversations; not generalisable. Optional detail; the post does not depend on it.

numbers.meaning: documented attempt to contact next of kin before surgery, pre-intervention, one hospital
next-of-kin section of Consent Form Four completed, before and after intervention

claims.claim: In a Cochrane review, peripheral nerve blocks reduced pain on movement within 30 minutes of being placed, by the equivalent of about 2.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale (high-certainty evidence).
claims.supporting_passage: "We included 49 trials (3061 participants; 1553 randomized to PNBs and 1508 to no nerve block (or sham block))." ... "Results of 11 trials with 503 participants show that PNBs reduced pain on movement within 30 minutes of block placement (standardized mean difference (SMD) -1.05, 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.25 to -0.86; equivalent to -2.5 on a scale from 0 to 10; high-certainty evidence)." Authors' conclusions: "PNBs reduce pain on movement within 30 minutes after block placement..."
claims.location: Abstract (Main results; Authors' conclusions)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with hip fracture (RCTs, 1981 to 2020) / peripheral nerve block / no block or sham, additional analgesia available to all / pain on movement / within 30 minutes of placement
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review of the trials found that a nerve block (an injection of local anaesthetic near the nerves to the hip) reduced pain on movement within half an hour by about 2.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale, compared with no block.
claims.qualifications: The 30-minute result comes from 11 of the 49 trials (503 people). Everyone could have other pain relief as well.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Effect size depended on local anaesthetic concentration.

numbers.meaning: whole review
pain-on-movement analysis
reduction in pain on movement within 30 minutes of placement (SMD -1.05)

claims.claim: Nerve blocks probably reduce chest infection and shorten the time to first getting out of bed by about 11 hours (moderate certainty, small numbers of trials); effects on death are uncertain.
claims.supporting_passage: "From three trials with 131 participants, PNBs probably reduce the risk for chest infection (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.89; NNTB 7, 95% CI 5 to 72; moderate-certainty evidence). Based on 11 trials with 617 participants, the effects of PNBs on mortality within six months are uncertain due to very serious imprecision (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.60; low-certainty evidence). From three trials with 208 participants, PNBs likely reduce time to first mobilization (mean difference (MD) -10.80 hours, 95% CI -12.83 to -8.77 hours; moderate-certainty evidence)."
claims.location: Abstract (Main results)
claims.pico_timeframe: As C03-06-a; chest infection, first mobilisation, 6-month mortality
claims.safe_wording: The same review found that blocks probably mean fewer chest infections and getting out of bed about 11 hours sooner, though these results come from only a few small trials. Whether blocks affect survival is uncertain.
claims.qualifications: Chest infection: 3 trials, 131 people; mobilisation: 3 trials, 208 people. Do not give the relative risk as 'times less likely'; if a number is needed use the NNT with its wide range (about 1 fewer infection for every 7 people treated, range 5 to 72) or avoid it. The review also reports fewer cases of acute confusion; delirium is an excluded topic, so leave it out.

numbers.meaning: earlier first mobilisation with a block; 3 trials, 208 people
chest infection; 3 trials, 131 people

claims.claim: People with dementia were often excluded from the nerve block trials.
claims.supporting_passage: "The average age of participants ranged from 59 to 89 years. People with dementia were often excluded from the included trials. Additional analgesia was available for all participants."
claims.location: Abstract (Main results)
claims.pico_timeframe: As above
claims.safe_wording: People with dementia were often left out of these trials, so the evidence is thinner for the people who may find it hardest to say they are in pain.
claims.qualifications: The second half of the safe wording is a reasonable inference; keep it modest or omit.

claims.claim: UK anaesthetic guidance recommends single-shot nerve blocks in the emergency department and again at the time of surgery, and notes that blocks reduce pain at rest and on movement, reduce time to getting moving and are not contraindicated in people on anticoagulants.
claims.supporting_passage: "Randomised controlled trials [25, 26], observational studies [19], consensus opinion [2], national audit initiatives [8] and systematic review [27] all support the widespread use of peripheral nerve blocks for analgesia on admission to hospital and in the early postoperative period. These are effective at reducing pain and quadriceps spasm at rest and on movement; reduce time to remobilisation; reduce opioid administration (to a patient population 40% of who have renal dysfunction and are at greater risk of postoperative delirium); and are not contra-indicated in anticoagulated patients [28]. The Working Party recommends that: 1Single shot nerve blocks should be provided in the Emergency Department and at the time of surgery (provided 6 h has passed between blocks) [27]. There is some evidence for their efficacy in providing pre-hospital analgesia [29]; 2Femoral or fascia iliaca blocks should be used, the latter possibly providing better incisional analgesia after surgery."
claims.location: Griffiths 2021 full text, 'Specific changes to the 2011 guidance' (analgesia)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK hip fracture patients, admission to early postoperative period
claims.safe_wording: The Association of Anaesthetists recommends a single-injection nerve block in the emergency department and another at the time of surgery.
claims.qualifications: The guideline says 'in the Emergency Department', not 'before X-ray'; the drawn sequence must not show the block before imaging unless labelled as one possible order. A second block needs at least 6 hours after the first.

numbers.meaning: minimum gap between ED block and block at surgery

claims.claim: NICE recommends considering nerve blocks if paracetamol and opioids are not enough before surgery, or to limit opioid dose, and asks that pain relief be enough to allow the movements needed for investigations, nursing care and rehabilitation.
claims.supporting_passage: "4.2.3 Analgesia ➢ Assess the patient's pain: • immediately upon presentation at hospital and • within 30 minutes of administering initial analgesia and • hourly until settled on the ward and • regularly as part of routine nursing observations throughout admission. ➢ Offer immediate analgesia to patients presenting at hospital with suspected hip fracture, including people with cognitive impairment. ➢ Ensure analgesia is sufficient to allow movements necessary for investigations (as indicated by the ability to tolerate passive external rotation of the leg), and for nursing care and rehabilitation." ... "➢ Consider adding nerve blocks if paracetamol and opioids do not provide sufficient preoperative pain relief, or to limit opioid dosage. Nerve blocks should be administered by trained personnel. Do not use nerve blocks as a substitute for early surgery."
claims.location: NICE full guideline section 4.2.3
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with suspected or confirmed hip fracture, preoperative
claims.safe_wording: NICE asks that pain relief be good enough for the person to be moved for X-rays, nursing care and rehabilitation, and says a nerve block should be considered when paracetamol and morphine-type drugs are not enough, or to reduce how much of them is needed.
claims.qualifications: NICE's nerve block recommendation is conditional ('consider'), not 'offer'. It was not changed in the 2023 update per the Age and Ageing commentary (live page not opened). NICE also says blocks are not a substitute for early surgery.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Association of Anaesthetists (2020) and Scottish standards are stronger (block as routine/first-line in ED).

numbers.meaning: NICE: reassess pain within 30 minutes of initial analgesia

claims.claim: The Scottish standards note that people with hip fracture often have little pain at rest but severe pain on movement, and make a fascia iliaca block the first-line choice in the emergency department.
claims.supporting_passage: "Standard 2: The 'big six' bundle is carried out in the emergency department (ED)" ... "4. Provide pain relief: all patients who sustain this painful injury must be offered analgesia. It is important to recognise that patients often have little pain on rest but severe pain on movement and for this reason a fascia iliaca block is the first-line choice."
claims.location: Scottish standards of care for hip fracture patients (v1.2, Sep 2025), Standard 2 rationale
claims.pico_timeframe: People with hip fracture in NHS Scotland emergency departments
claims.safe_wording: Scotland's national hip fracture standards point out that people often have little pain lying still but severe pain when moved, and name a nerve block (fascia iliaca block) as the first choice for pain relief in the emergency department.
claims.qualifications: Cite as a published standard; do not mention or imply audit results (Alasdair chairs the audit).

claims.claim: A single-injection block lasts hours, not the whole wait for surgery: a review puts a single-shot fascia iliaca block with bupivacaine at about 8 hours of pain relief, and trial evidence in the emergency department measured benefit up to 4 hours.
claims.supporting_passage: Verbeek 2021 abstract: "Single-shot FICB is faster to place, yet providing about 8 h of analgesia when bupivacaine is used. Continuous FICB provides prolonged titratable analgesia..." Makkar 2021 abstract: "A significant difference in pain relief at rest and on movement started within 30 min and lasted till 4 h of the block." ... "However, the quality of evidence is low and additional trials are necessary." Griffiths 2021: "Single shot nerve blocks should be provided in the Emergency Department and at the time of surgery (provided 6 h has passed between blocks)".
claims.location: Verbeek 2021 abstract; Makkar 2021 abstract (Results, Conclusions); Griffiths 2021 analgesia section
claims.pico_timeframe: Hip fracture, single-shot fascia iliaca block, emergency department; pain relief duration
claims.safe_wording: A single injection does not last until the operation. It usually gives several hours of relief (one review suggests about 8 hours with a long-acting local anaesthetic), which is why UK guidance also advises another block at the time of surgery. Giving it early in the emergency department covers the X-ray, the move to the ward and the first hours of nursing care.
claims.qualifications: The 8-hour figure comes from a narrative review and depends on drug and dose; trial evidence (low certainty) measured benefit only to 4 hours. Do not say it 'spares pain at every later move' (judge's concern). The link between the ED block and the second block at surgery is guideline structure, not a stated rationale; phrase as 'UK guidance also advises', not 'because'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Pasquier 2019 (small RCT, seen in Consensus, not used) found no added benefit when pain was already low after prehospital morphine.

numbers.meaning: approximate duration of single-shot FICB with bupivacaine (narrative review)
duration over which trials measured benefit (meta-analysis of 11 trials, 895 patients, low certainty)

claims.claim: A person with a hip fracture typically goes through several transfers (floor, ambulance trolley, emergency department trolley, X-ray table, ward bed), each of which moves the fracture.
claims.supporting_passage: No source found or opened that describes or counts the transfers. NICE (DRIVE:1pftOMXMI_OAkTBofH11t6ayryZ2F-YXb) supports the related point that analgesia must allow 'movements necessary for investigations ... and for nursing care'.
claims.location: n/a
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: On the way from home to a ward bed, a person with a broken hip is usually lifted or slid several times: onto an ambulance trolley, onto a hospital trolley, for the X-ray and into bed.
claims.qualifications: Present as a generic, typical description, not a measured count; no numbers. The visual must not place the ED block before the X-ray as fact (in UK practice the block is given in the ED, often after the fracture is confirmed); show it as 'in the emergency department'. Prehospital blocks exist in some services ('some evidence for their efficacy', Griffiths 2021) but are not routine; do not imply they are.

claims.claim: In the REGAIN trial (1600 previously walking adults aged 50 and over, 46 US and Canadian hospitals), death or inability to walk about 3 metres at 60 days occurred in 18.5% with spinal and 18.0% with general anaesthesia.
claims.supporting_passage: "We conducted a pragmatic, randomized superiority trial to evaluate spinal anesthesia as compared with general anesthesia in previously ambulatory patients 50 years of age or older who were undergoing surgery for hip fracture at 46 U.S. and Canadian hospitals. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive spinal or general anesthesia. The primary outcome was a composite of death or an inability to walk approximately 10 ft (3 m) independently or with a walker or cane at 60 days after randomization." ... "Among patients in the modified intention-to-treat population for whom data were available, the composite primary outcome occurred in 132 of 712 patients (18.5%) in the spinal anesthesia group and 132 of 733 (18.0%) in the general anesthesia group (relative risk, 1.03; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.84 to 1.27; P = 0.83)."
claims.location: Abstract (Methods, Results)
claims.pico_timeframe: Previously ambulatory adults 50+ having hip fracture surgery, 46 US/Canadian hospitals / spinal anaesthesia / general anaesthesia / death or inability to walk ~3 m independently or with a walker or cane / 60 days
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 1,600 people who could walk before their hip fracture, about 18 in 100 had died or could not walk across a small room (about 3 metres) two months later, whether they had a spinal or a general anaesthetic.
claims.qualifications: Composite outcome; say what it combines. US and Canadian hospitals; only people who could walk before the fracture. Did not show a clear difference (not 'proved equal').

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported: HIP ATTACK co-primary results (abstract), its secondary benefits (faster mobilisation, shorter stay, no harm) via the Association of Anaesthetists 2020 full text, the Ontario association (Pincus 2017) and the NICE/36-hour targets. Wording conditions: say accelerated surgery 'did not clearly reduce' deaths or major complications, not that speed has no benefit; include one line on the secondary benefits; treat Pincus as an association; replace 'faster than many hospitals achieve' with 'half the comparison group had surgery within about 24 hours' (C03-17-e). Pain benefit not verified; do not claim it. Delirium result optional at most (topic excluded).

The NICE list, the echocardiography advice and the antiplatelet position are all sourced, but the framing and two claims must change. NICE frames the list as problems to treat immediately so that surgery is not delayed, not as reasons that justify delay. The angle's statement that 'medically unfit' delays 'often turn out' to be waits for tests or drugs is unsupported. The antiplatelet advice is the Association of Anaesthetists' 2011 guidance as restated in its 2020 update (Appendix S1 not opened), backed by observational meta-analysis. DOAC timing 'depends on drug, dose and kidney function' was not verified.
candidates.revised_angle: Teaching round built on NICE's own framing: find and treat nine correctable problems straight away so they don't delay surgery; routine tests that won't change the operation or anaesthetic should not hold it up (NICE); UK anaesthetic guidance does not recommend waiting for an echocardiogram and has advised since 2011 not to delay for aspirin or clopidogrel; 36 hours is enough to correct most problems if work starts at once, and the team should say what needs to happen and document it (Association of Anaesthetists 2020; Scottish standard). DOACs are the exception with their own timing guidance: in 2018 almost all DOAC users in England and Wales waited over 36 hours, so ask the anaesthetist or orthogeriatrician for the plan. The 'name the problem and the time' close is marked as 'we should'.

candidates.reason: Key claim sourced: England and Wales (Wade and Kitzinger 2019; Orr and Baruah 2018; Zalmay 2021, PubMed-indexed hip fracture source as the editor asked): the decision-maker is an LPA for health and welfare or court deputy, otherwise usually the responsible clinician in the person's best interests, with family consulted. Scotland (Edwardson and Baruah 2018): a certificate of incapacity gives general authority, but a welfare attorney's consent must be sought where reasonable and practicable, and past and present wishes must be taken into account. Conditions: the guardian-can-consent wording was not verified in an opened source, so limit to welfare attorney unless the editor accepts the statute; do not describe Northern Ireland; GMC guidance not opened and dropped; do not claim how often relatives are asked to sign. C03-18 is therefore not needed as the fallback.

Evidence is strong (Cochrane pain-on-movement result, high certainty; Association of Anaesthetists recommends ED blocks; Scottish standard makes the fascia iliaca block first-line because pain is on movement; NICE asks for pain relief sufficient for movements needed for investigations and nursing care). The core insight overstates, though: a single-shot block lasts hours (about 8 h in one review; trials measured 4 h), so it cannot spare pain 'at every later move'. NICE's own block recommendation is 'consider', not 'offer'. The transfer sequence is unsourced and must stay generic, with the block shown in the ED rather than before the X-ray.
candidates.revised_angle: Pain after a hip fracture is mostly on movement, and the first hours involve several lifts and slides. A nerve block given in the emergency department reduces pain on movement within 30 minutes (Cochrane) and lasts several hours, which covers the X-ray, the transfer to the ward and early nursing care; UK anaesthetic guidance also advises another block at the time of surgery. Families can ask: has a nerve block been offered? Staff can time it before the moves rather than after. Note that people with dementia were often excluded from the trials.

candidates.reason: Reserve and named fallback for C03-09; not needed because C03-09's key claim is sourced. All essential claims are supported if it is used later: REGAIN primary composite and components, crossover (about 1 in 6), one-year outcomes similar (Vail 2024, which answers the judge's 'longer-term outcomes' point), the result that went the other way (more early pain and 60-day analgesic use with spinal; Neuman 2022) and the NICE recommendation to offer a choice. Conditions: say what the composite combines; population is previously walking adults in the US and Canada; exclusions such as advanced dementia were not verified, so do not state them; RAGA not verified and dropped.
